title: The Journey of a Water Droplet
subtitle: Understanding the Water Cycle
description: Follow a single water droplet as it travels through all four stages of the water cycle — from ocean to sky and back again.

segments.label: Evaporation
segments.description: The sun heats the ocean surface, causing water molecules to gain energy and rise as invisible vapor.

segments.label: Condensation
segments.description: Water vapor cools as it rises into the atmosphere, condensing around tiny particles to form clouds.

segments.label: Precipitation
segments.description: When cloud droplets combine and grow heavy enough, they fall as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.

segments.label: Collection
segments.description: Water flows across the land into rivers, lakes, and back to the ocean, completing the cycle.

hotspots.label: Dust

assessment.instructions: Answer the following questions about the water cycle based on what you just experienced.

levels.label: Recall & Understand
levels.description: Test your memory and understanding of the water cycle facts.

items.question: What causes water vapor to form clouds?
options: Water vapor is heated further by the sun
Water vapor cools and condenses around tiny particles
Wind pushes water droplets together
Gravity pulls water vapor into cloud shapes
items.explanation: When water vapor rises and cools, it condenses around condensation nuclei (tiny particles like dust, pollen, and sea salt) to form cloud droplets.

items.question: What provides the energy that drives evaporation?
options: Wind energy
Gravitational potential energy
Solar radiation (heat from the sun)
Chemical reactions in the water
items.explanation: The sun's heat provides the thermal energy needed for water molecules to break free from the liquid surface and become water vapor.

items.question: Which of these is NOT a type of precipitation?
options: Rain
Evaporation
Snow
Hail
items.explanation: Evaporation is the process of water turning from liquid to gas — the opposite of precipitation. Rain, snow, and hail are all forms of precipitation.

levels.label: Apply
levels.description: Apply what you learned to new situations you haven't seen before.

items.question: A puddle of water disappears on a hot, sunny day with no rain. What happened to the water?
options: The ground absorbed all of it permanently
The water evaporated — solar energy turned it into water vapor
The wind blew it away as liquid
It was consumed by bacteria in the soil
items.explanation: The sun's heat caused the water in the puddle to evaporate, turning it into invisible water vapor that rose into the atmosphere — the same process that happens to ocean water.

items.question: If you put a cold glass outside on a humid day and water droplets form on the outside, which part of the water cycle does this most closely resemble?
options: Precipitation — water is falling onto the glass
Evaporation — water is leaving the glass surface
Condensation — water vapor in the air is cooling on the glass surface
Collection — water is being collected by the glass
items.explanation: The cold glass surface cools the warm, moist air around it, causing the water vapor to condense into liquid droplets — exactly like water vapor condensing into clouds when it reaches cooler altitudes.

items.question: A city at the base of a mountain range gets much more rain than a city on the other side. Why?
options: The mountain blocks the sun, making it colder
Moist air rises over the mountain, cools, and precipitates on the windward side
The mountain produces its own water through geological processes
Rivers from the mountain carry more water to that side
items.explanation: This is the 'rain shadow' effect — moist air is forced upward by the mountain, cools (condensation), and releases precipitation on the windward side, leaving the other side dry.

levels.label: Implement
levels.description: Demonstrate your understanding by constructing and ordering concepts.

items.question: Arrange the 4 stages of the water cycle in the correct order, starting from the ocean.

items_to_order.label: Collection — water flows back to ocean
Evaporation — sun heats water to vapor

items.explanation: The water cycle follows this order: Evaporation (water becomes vapor) → Condensation (vapor forms clouds) → Precipitation (water falls) → Collection (water returns to bodies of water).

items.question: Put these events in order from the perspective of a single water molecule's journey.

items_to_order.label: You cool down and stick to a dust particle in a cloud
You sit in the ocean, absorbing sunlight
You grow heavy with other droplets and fall as rain
You gain enough energy to break free and float upward
You land in a stream and flow back to the sea

items.explanation: A water molecule's journey: sits in ocean → gains energy and evaporates → cools and condenses in a cloud → grows heavy and precipitates → flows through streams back to the ocean.
